item.title: Tk5cr per MP: LGD’s proposal sparks questions over source and accountability
item.description:
The Local Government Division has sought a special development allocation of Tk5 crore for each member of parliament (MP), Tk1,500 crore in all for 300 MPs, to meet what it calls the urgent needs of people in their constituencies.
But the money is proposed to come not from a new source, but from the annual development funds of upazila parishads and city corporations, raising questions over the impact on local government’s own development activities and the role of MPs in grassroots decisions.
With allegations of irregularities, nepotism and politicisation having surfaced over earlier allocations to MPs, the debate now centres less on whether the money is needed than on where it comes from, who will control its spending, and who will be held accountable.
According to Local Government Ministry sources, Local Government Division Senior Secretary Md Shahidul Hassan sent two separate letters to Finance Division Secretary Dr Md Khairuzzaman Mazumder on November 10.
The proposal seeks Tk1,320 crore for 264 MPs outside city corporation areas, at Tk5 crore each, and Tk180 crore for 36 MPs in city corporation areas, bringing the total to Tk1,500 crore.
The letters state that the money will be spent on renovating educational and religious institutions, providing assistance to poor and meritorious students, the welfare of helpless people, and sports and cultural activities.
The local government secretary noted in the letter that people’s expectations have increased following the restoration of the democratic system after long-standing deprivation and discrimination. MPs hear about people’s small but urgent problems when visiting their constituencies, he wrote, but these needs cannot be met with the limited allocations available under the existing discretionary fund.
A senior Local Government Division official confirmed to Dhaka Tribune that the letters have been sent to the Finance Ministry. Speaking on condition of anonymity, he said the allocation currently available to MPs in the discretionary fund is very insignificant, and questioned how much of a constituency’s needs can be met with only Tk5 lakh.
He said the letters were sent with the consent of MPs from both the ruling and opposition parties, and that opposition MPs will receive the same amount as ruling party MPs.
“During the Awami League’s tenure, there were instances of special development allocations of Tk15 crore and later Tk20 crore for MPs. Compared to that, this is much less. Besides, all MPs will use this money in the interest of developing their respective areas,” he said.
However, alongside the argument for equal allocations, questions have arisen over how justified it is to give the same amount to all constituencies when population, poverty, infrastructure gaps and actual needs vary.
Special development allocations for MPs are not new. Allocations of Tk15 crore and Tk20 crore per MP were made in the past under constituency-based rural infrastructure development projects. The current government also has an initiative to undertake separate projects worth Tk50 crore per MP over five years through the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED), covering roads, bridges and other infrastructure prioritised by MPs. Development researchers have therefore questioned how the new Tk5 crore proposal will be coordinated with earlier initiatives.
In a 2020 study, Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) reviewed 628 development works in 50 parliamentary constituencies. It found instances of low-quality work, unethical transactions between contractors and those concerned, and political influence, along with a lack of transparency and supervision from planning to implementation.
TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman said analysis of past experience and data showed that the bulk of block allocations was used for politicisation in the name of development, creating opportunities for widespread irregularities, corruption, embezzlement and wastage of public money. “The expectation from the current government is that it will move away from this past practice,” he said.
Experts have also raised concerns about the source of the money, which is proposed to come from the annual development funds of upazila parishads and city corporations. They fear this may curtail local governments’ own priority-based development activities.
Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution establish the basis for the responsibilities and powers of local government institutions, while the primary constitutional responsibilities of MPs are to enact laws and ensure government accountability. Existing laws, however, give MPs an advisory role in local development.
The Local Government Division’s budget for the current 2026-27 fiscal year is Tk40,246 crore, approximately 9% lower than the previous fiscal year’s revised allocation. Amid this, demands have been raised to assess the impact of reallocating funds from existing development funds.
Political analyst Ruhin Hossain Prince told Dhaka Tribune: “First, in my view, the development allocations provided for MPs and ministers for local development are not supported by our Constitution. In other words, this is contradictory to the Constitution. Second, what we say about strengthening local government is also affected. Third, such allocations create opportunities for MPs to assume the role of landlords.”
“Since we are trying to move towards democracy, local government must be strengthened. If public participation and accountability cannot be ensured, the benefits of democracy will not reach the actual people. Considering that, it is necessary to stay away from this kind of allocation and keep MPs away from it as well. This money should be spent through local government while ensuring complete transparency,” he added.
Those concerned say that if the allocation is approved, it must be made clear who will be responsible for selecting projects or beneficiaries, releasing funds, implementation and auditing. In particular, a policy is needed on whether the money will be spent on MPs’ recommendations or whether MPs will be able to make spending decisions directly.
They warn that unless spending information is made public, local participation is ensured, independent audits are conducted and effective action is taken against irregularities, the special allocations risk becoming a tool for political influence.
With the proposal justified by the need to meet people’s urgent needs, how the source of the funds and control over their spending will be determined is now the key question.

item.title: BGB: Tk273.37 crore smuggled goods, drugs seized in October
item.description:

During the month, huge quantities of narcotics were seized, including 40,45,412 Yaba tablets, 8.097kg of crystal meth (ice), 941 grams of heroin, 1,201 bottles of Phensedyl, 11,307 bottles of foreign liquor, and 1,564kg of hemp.
Besides, 219 smugglers were arrested, while legal action was taken against 114 Bangladeshis, seven Indians, and 350 Myanmar nationals for illegal border crossing.

item.title: Bangladesh to withdraw from global treaty on shipbreaking waste management
item.description:
In 1986, a ship named Pelican, loaded with fly ash, set sail from the port of Philadelphia in the United States. The ship drifted in the sea for two years.

No country allowed it to anchor because it carried 14,000 tonnes of polluted ash harmful to the environment and human health.

On a morning in October 1988, the captain of the ship announced that they had dumped the ash off the coast of a country, but he did not mention the name of the country. It was later revealed that the country was Haiti.

This led to a storm of protests worldwide. The detailed account of this incident is documented in a report titled "Planet of the Year: A Sinking Mess" on the 2 January 1989 issue of the world-renowned Time Magazine.

Facing global protests, on 22 March 1989, the United Nations initiated the ‘Basel Convention’ to regulate waste movement from one country to another. Its full name is ‘The Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal. ’ A total of 170 countries, including Bangladesh, have signed the convention.

However, at the request of shipbreaking industry owners, the Bangladesh government has decided to withdraw from the Basel Convention’s section on shipbreaking.

In August, the cabinet formed a committee to review the laws, rules, policies, and related aspects of the shipbreaking industry, with Environment, Forest, and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo as the head.

On 29 September, this committee decided to exit the Basel Convention and follow the Hong Kong Convention in the matter of shipbreaking.

It is noteworthy that the Basel Convention establishes control over international waste movement. On the other hand, the Hong Kong Convention primarily deals with safe shipbreaking-related issues in yards.

Mohammad Mohsin, the president of the Bangladesh Ship Breakers and Ship Recyclers Association, told Prothom Alo that efforts are being made to make the shipbreaking industry safe by following the Hong Kong Convention. For this, each yard is required to invest Tk 1.5 billion to 2 billion.

Mohammad Mohsin stated, “Hong Kong Convention and Basel Convention are like two different physicians for the same disease. We want any one of them to cure this disease. In this case, we have requested the government to follow the Hong Kong Convention because the International Labour Organisation (ILO), the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), and those who manage shipping lines are all linked with the Hong Kong Convention.”

However, environmental experts say that the Hong Kong Convention does not consider ships as waste. Therefore, shipbreaking industry owners prefer the Hong Kong Convention.

Syeda Rizwana Hasan, the chief executive of the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA), told Prothom Alo that the shipbreaking industry is a tactic to smuggle developed countries' waste under the guise of shipbreaking; which can be proven through the Basel Convention. That’s why shipbreaking industry owners do not want to remain under the Basel Convention.

What’s in the Basel Convention

According to Article 2 of the Basel Convention, expired ships are considered hazardous waste. For example, a ship suitable for sea travel but its owner decides not to use it for commercial transport and wants to sell it to a yard in Bangladesh for breaking. In such a situation, the ship would be considered waste under the Basel Convention.

The Basel Convention does not ban the import or scrapping of all expired ships; rather, it imposes control over transboundary movements of ships defined as waste and those carrying hazardous waste.

According to Article 6 of the Basel Convention, before exporting hazardous waste, the exporting country must inform the importing country about the waste. It would then have to obtain written consent from the importing country. An agreement between the exporting and importing countries must exist for the environmentally sound disposal of waste.

Article 8 states that if the waste cannot be disposed of according to the agreement, the exporting country must take back the waste.

Environment, Forest, and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo told Prothom Alo, “Everything relating to shipbreaking is overseen by the IMO. The Hong Kong Convention is under the IMO. Our green yards are also constructed in light of the Hong Kong Convention.”

Assuring that there will be no problems with waste management, the minister mentioned that each green yard has specialised places for storing waste. Some waste is sold to vendors licensed by the Department of Environment. In addition, a TSDF (Treatment, Storage, and Disposal Facility) for shipbreaking waste management is being constructed in Mirsarai.

What international experts are saying

The Brussels-based international organisation ‘NGO Shipbreaking Platform’ has been working for a long time to ensure a safe working environment for workers in the shipbreaking industry.

In response to written questions from Prothom Alo, Ingvild Jenssen, the founder and executive director of the platform, stated that Bangladesh needs to adhere to the Basel Convention. This global convention is crucial to stopping the dumping of toxic waste and protecting the environment and human health from the harm of hazardous substances.

She mentioned that if Bangladesh moves away from the Basel Convention concerning abandoned ships, the marine ecosystem and coastal environment will be at greater risk, and coastal residents will be in danger.

Jenssen advised that both the Basel and Hong Kong Conventions could be effectively implemented alongside each other; rather, if both conventions are enforced together, the protection of the environment and workers would be stronger. She pointed out that the regulations for safe and environmentally sound shipbreaking in the Hong Kong Convention are weak.

Why the Hong Kong Convention is weak

The Basel Convention was established under the initiative of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), whereas the Hong Kong Convention falls under the United Nations Maritime Organization (IMO).
The International Chamber of Shipping and European Shipowners conducted an independent study last June through the Netherlands-based research organisation CE Delft.

This study, titled ‘Assessing Global Standard For Ship Recycling, ’ identified three major weaknesses of the Hong Kong Convention. These are the approval and inspection of shipbreaking yards, subsequent management of hazardous waste, and the scope of the list of hazardous materials.

The study states that the convention does not ban open beach shipbreaking methods in Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan. There is a risk that oil, heavy metals, and toxic waste may mix with soil and water due to shipbreaking on beaches.

According to the Hong Kong Convention, the responsibility for managing hazardous waste primarily falls on the importing countries. Ship owners or the source countries of waste are not held accountable for the waste. However, under the Basel Convention, the exporting country must inform the importing country before sending waste and obtain a letter of consent.

item.title: US suggested Kyiv cede land to Russia in exchange for joining NATO, Zelensky says
item.description:
UKRAINE-CRISIS/ZELENSKIY-TALKS

Washington has suggested Ukraine cede land to Russia in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments released Saturday, adding that it indicated his country's ties with the Western military alliance are "back on the agenda".

Zelensky also warned the Kremlin was "betting everything" on this winter's military campaign.

Moscow has pounded Ukraine in the run-up to the colder months, with Russian President Vladimir Putin showing no sign of backing down.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met both Putin and Zelensky separately on Thursday after two days of talks with their delegations in Abu Dhabi, which ended with no breakthrough.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said.

US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine

"After providing Ukraine with this kind of defence support, seeing this kind of development of our army and this strength in our defence, they cannot simply let Ukraine go," he added.

He said the discussion showed that "NATO is back on the agenda" for Ukraine.

Ukraine has long sought to enter the military alliance, which Moscow has considered a red line.

NATO and Washington have not yet commented directly on Zelensky's account.

Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, later posted on X that media had reported "maximalist propositions proposed by both sides, along with strong political rhetoric".

"However, we are determined to continue the hard work, maintain the confidentiality necessary for sensitive negotiations, and find a pathway to end this horrible war," he said, adding "several new ideas emerged from the discussions and are now being explored."

This week's meetings have led to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war.

In Dublin on Friday, Europe chose five countries -- France, Germany, Italy, the UK and Poland -- to send representatives to the talks.

Russia meanwhile continued its bombardment of Ukraine on Saturday, with deadly strikes in the eastern city of Pavlohrad and in a village near Zaporizhzhia, which is now just a few dozen kilometres from the front line.

Kyiv seeks guarantees

Zelensky said Kyiv was discussing security guarantees with Western partners and that Ukrainians would ultimately decide whether to accept any deal.

He insisted Ukraine would not recognise any land seized by Moscow's troops as Russian.

Russia has consistently said Kyiv joining NATO is a red line and in 2022 launched its invasion saying the West planned to incorporate Ukraine into the alliance.

Trump's administration has for almost two years tried to reach a breakthrough in talks between Russia and Ukraine.

The Kremlin has also ruled out foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine and wider ceasefires.

But Putin earlier this week proposed a "humanitarian" mission to the eastern town of Kostyantynivka, which Moscow announced it had seized in the summer but where Kyiv says fighting continues.

Zelensky said the proposal was a bid to advance Russian gains in Donetsk. "Their next steps will be our other cities in Donbas," he said.

Russian troops have inched westwards but have been unable to seize the whole of the Donetsk region.

'First, end the war'

Russia has tried to reframe negotiations on ending the war -- Europe's worst since World War II -- into a conversation on the continent's wider security.

In 2021, before its Ukraine invasion, Moscow issued an ultimatum to the West to pull back NATO troops from eastern Europe.

Moscow's chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, this week called for a "new, modern Yalta", drawing criticism from European leaders.

Zelensky warned that any discussion of wider security arrangements should come only after the war has ended.

European leaders have reacted coolly to the proposal for a new security architecture.

"We do not need to discuss that, it already exists," Germany's Friedrich Merz said Friday.

French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that "those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it" and, by extension, all of Europe.

"That is the spirit of defeat. That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France's position," Macron said.

"Helping Ukraine defend itself is protecting France and the French," he added.

Climate adaptation funding shortfall puts Bangladesh under pressure
item.description:
Even after 17 years of Cyclone Aila, the homestead of Md Zia Gain and his wife, Shamima Begum, in Mothbari village of Koyra upazila, Khulna, remains submerged beneath the waters of the Shakbaria River.

A nearly three-kilometre-long and 250-metre-wide channel, formed by tidal currents after an embankment collapsed, has swallowed their home. They now live on the slope of the embankment of the river.

The house of Minoti Sana, a woman in her 60's from the same village, also once stood in what is now the middle of the river. Her land has remained unrecovered since Cyclone Aila.

Ismail Gazi, Yunus Ali and Ilias Gazi, along with many other villagers, share similar stories. They lost their homesteads and have been living on the slopes of embankments for the past 17 years.

Natural disasters are nothing new in Bangladesh. However, the loss of homes, rising salinity and shortages of safe drinking water in coastal areas continue to transform people's lives over the long term. How to address these challenges is being discussed at the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye.

The United Nations Environment Programme's (UNEP) Adaptation Gap Report 2026, published ahead of the conference, highlights the shortfall in climate adaptation finance.

How much funding is needed for adaptation?

According to Bangladesh's third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), the country needs US$8.5 billion annually to implement its adaptation priorities. The same document estimates that the average annual flow of funding for adaptation in the country stands at around US$4 billion.

This leaves an annual shortfall of US$4.5 billion, equivalent to approximately Tk 561.38 billion (Tk 56,138 crore), at an exchange rate of Tk 124.75 per US dollar.

NDC 3.0 states that Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing requirements could rise to between US$12 billion and US$14 billion by 2035.

At the same exchange rate, this would amount to approximately Tk 1,497 billion to Tk 1,746.5 billion (Tk 149,700 crore to Tk 174,650 crore).

Growing needs, insufficient funding

Bangladesh's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) estimates that the country will need a total of US$230 billion to implement 113 initiatives between 2023 and 2050. This amounts to an average of approximately US$8.5 billion annually over 27 years.

The initiatives cover various sectors, including water, agriculture, fisheries and livestock, urban development, disaster management, biodiversity and institutional capacity-building.

UNEP's report draws its estimate of Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing needs of US$12–14 billion by 2035 from the country's third NDC.

The report also states that international public adaptation finance from developed countries to developing nations stood at US$28.7 billion in 2024, an increase of just US$1 billion from the previous year.

The annual adaptation financing needs of developing countries could reach approximately US$305 billion by 2035. This estimate uses 2024 prices and excludes the requirements of the private sector. Including private-sector needs could almost double the total requirement.

At COP30, countries called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035. According to UNEP's estimates, even if this target is achieved, it would meet only 20 to 29 per cent of the potential adaptation financing needs of developing countries.

The nature of the financing also matters. In 2024, loans accounted for 55 per cent of international public adaptation finance for developing countries, while grants made up 44 per cent. Nearly half of the loans came on market-based or non-concessional terms.

Experts say Bangladesh needs more grants and low-interest, long-term financing to meet its adaptation costs without placing further pressure on public debt.

Climate finance expert Haseeb Muhammad Irfanullah told Prothom Alo, "Reports published ahead of the COP conferences help us understand changes in the nature and flow of adaptation finance and provide useful insights for negotiations. However, a significant funding gap remains in the flow of finance from developed to developing countries."

Bangladesh still bears the cost of climate damage

According to UNEP's report, Bangladesh allocated at least US$400 million from its revenue budget to the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund between 2010 and the 2017–18 fiscal year. During this period, the authorities approved 512 projects across 18 ministries.

At least 45 per cent of the fund, or more than US$180 million, went towards adaptation activities. However, this amount remains inadequate compared with the country's potential annual requirement of US$12–14 billion.

The Climate Budget Report for the 2026–27 fiscal year estimates climate-related expenditure of Tk 517.46 billion (Tk 51,746 crore) across 25 ministries and divisions. Of this amount, Tk 389.06 billion (Tk 38,906 crore) is allocated to adaptation.

The national budget also proposes an allocation of Tk 1 billion (Tk 100 crore) for the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund.

However, the overall figure for climate-related expenditure does not represent a separate allocation for new adaptation projects. Rather, it reflects climate-related spending identified within the budgets of various ministries and divisions.

Adaptation can reduce climate risks, but it cannot prevent all losses and damage. In the first funding round of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, 119 developing countries applied for US$2.8 billion.

However, the fund initially had only US$342 million, equivalent to around one-eighth of the total demand. Complex application procedures and limited institutional capacity also pose barriers to accessing support.

Farah Anjum, Bangladesh country lead at the Global Strategic Communications Council, who is attending COP31, told Prothom Alo, "Although Bangladesh faces significant climate risks, its contribution to global emissions is low. Yet the country has to bear much of the substantial cost of adaptation from its own resources. Developed countries should go beyond their existing commitments and provide accessible grant-based financing, technology transfer and technical assistance. They must also ensure that allocated funds reach vulnerable communities and effectively reduce climate-related losses and damage."

item.title: 294 murders a month on average as 2,938 murder cases filed in 10 months
item.description:
Sheikh Zakir Hossain, a leader of ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), was shot dead inside his shop at Rupsa upazila in Khulna on Thursday night. Over the past 22 days, six people have been killed and another six injured in shootings in Khulna. 

Such killings are not confined to Khulna alone; rather, they are taking place across the country. A total of 2,938 murder cases were filed nationwide in the first 10 months of this year, averaging nearly 294 a month.

Alongside murders, incidents of extortion, robbery, mugging and the public use of firearms have heightened concerns over law and order in the country. 

People from various walks of life say the law-and-order situation has yet to improve as expected, even eight months after the government took office. The police, however, say law and order collapsed following the mass uprising but the situation has been gradually improving.

Analysing the killings and related data, officials involved in investigations say most murders stemmed from political violence, extortion, attempts to establish dominance, youth gangs and disputes over control of the drug trade. Many others were the result of domestic violence.

An analysis of case records from the police headquarters shows that 170,101 cases involving various crimes were filed across the country between January and October this year. A total of 181,673 cases were filed in the whole of the previous year. Besides murder cases, 417 robbery cases, 1,519 cases of banditry and 867 kidnapping cases were filed in the first 10 months of this year.

According to police headquarters data, 218 murder cases were filed in Dhaka over the past 10 months, the highest figure among the eight metropolitan police areas. Most recently, 19 murder cases were filed in October, compared with 31 in September. 

A single case is sometimes filed over multiple incidents. Therefore, the number of cases does not necessarily reflect the actual number of crimes committed.

An analysis of case records from the eight metropolitan police units and nine police ranges shows that Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) recorded the highest number of murder cases among the metropolitan areas, with 218 in the past 10 months. Among the nine ranges, Dhaka Range recorded the highest number, with 673 murder cases, followed by Chattogram Range with 571.

Kamarum Munira, spokesperson for police headquarters and an assistant inspector general (AIG), told Prothom Alo that the police were taking a range of measures to prevent murders and bring perpetrators to justice. 

These included identifying crime-prone areas, keeping criminals under intelligence surveillance, recovering illegal firearms, arresting criminals and goons, and conducting regular raids, she added.

The police headquarters spokesperson further said instructions had been issued to promptly register cases involving every murder, collect forensic evidence and identify perpetrators through investigations.

Kamarum Munira added that the recent killings in Khulna were being treated as a matter of particular concern. A decision had been taken to conduct special joint operations involving law enforcement agencies to curb crime and extortion there. Other initiatives included strengthening checkpoints, patrols and intelligence surveillance on major roads, as well as launching drives against unregistered motorcycles.

218 murders in Dhaka

In April, top criminal Khandaker Naim Ahmed Titon was shot dead in broad daylight in the capital's New Market area. On 9 November, a young woman named Sanjida Akter Ima, 22, was strangled to death at a house in Uttarkhan, Dhaka.

According to police headquarters data, 218 murder cases were filed in Dhaka over the past 10 months, the highest figure among the eight metropolitan police areas. Most recently, 19 murder cases were filed in October, compared with 31 in September. 

The murders of four members of the same family in Rangpur, five members of a family in Kapasia, Gazipur, and a mother and her three daughters in Lakshmipur also drew nationwide attention.

DMP officials say between 20 and 30 murders take place every month across the jurisdiction of its 50 police stations.

Notable murders outside Dhaka

Several high-profile murders have taken place in different parts of the country over the past 10 months. Most recently, BNP leader and brick-and-sand trader Mohammad Zakir Hossain was shot dead inside a shop in the village of Sholpo Bahirdia in Rupsa, Khulna, on Thursday night.

Speaking at his funeral prayers (namaz-e-ianaza), Nazrul Islam Manju, administrator of Khulna City Corporation and a BNP leader, said Khulna had become engulfed in crimes, with murders, extortion and drug trading rampant. 

People were being killed for speaking out against these activities, he said. He called for joint operations to arrest listed criminals.

Between 22 October and 12 November, at least 13 shooting incidents took place in Khulna over 22 days. In one incident, criminals fired blank shots at a clinic after demanding extortion money. Six people were killed and another six injured in the shootings. Three more people were killed in attacks involving sharp weapons and beatings. 

In all, nine people were murdered in Khulna during the 22-day period: five in Khulna city, three in Rupsa and one in Dumuria upazilas. Up to 12 November this year, 39 murders had been recorded in Khulna city and 40 across the district.

Earlier, on 18 September, Ishayat Shahriar, also known as Apratim, 13, son of Nahida Begum, an associate professor in the Department of Bangla at Comilla University, was killed by members of a youth gang. The incident sparked widespread discussion across the country.

At around 8:30 pm on 15 October, journalist Lutfozzaman Alif Fakir, 44, was shot dead in Netrokona. Alif had reported on smuggling, drug and arms trafficking along the border, as well as local irregularities and wrongdoing. He regularly published photographs and videos exposing these activities. There are allegations that he was targeted and killed for his reporting.

The murders of four members of the same family in Rangpur, five members of a family in Kapasia, Gazipur, and a mother and her three daughters in Lakshmipur also drew nationwide attention.

item.title: More than half of Bangladesh’s births are now C-sections
item.description:
More than half of the babies born in Bangladesh now arrive through caesarean section.
But how many of those operations are truly necessary?
According to the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF, 51.8% of deliveries in the country now take place through the caesarean method, nearly three times the rate of 12 years ago. The World Health Organization (WHO) says caesarean sections should not be performed without medical necessity, and that a rate of 10% to 15% at the population level is the most appropriate.
The question has become a point of sharp disagreement. Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain says the trend of unnecessary operations has increased at an alarming rate, and alleges that some private clinics and broker networks frighten families into them.
Doctors say they try for normal delivery, that a caesarean is sometimes medically essential, and that some mothers themselves ask for one.
Experts say each pregnancy must be judged on its own circumstances, and that ensuring hospitals are accountable is now a major challenge.
Two days before the last Eid-ul-Azha, at around 7:45am, Fahmid Ahmed (pseudonym) was admitted to a private hospital in the capital with his pregnant wife. Throughout the pregnancy they had been under the care of a doctor at that hospital. Both the mother and the unborn child were in good physical condition, and the couple were mentally prepared for childbirth through the normal process.
Immediately after admission, they were asked, “Have you come for an operation?” The couple were surprised and said they had come for a normal delivery.
A new experience then began. Every now and then, the hospital’s assistant doctors would come to the pregnant mother and say, “Normal delivery is very painful”, “It is very difficult”, and “There will be a lot of complications”. At one point her husband protested: “Why are you saying such things? Where you should be giving encouragement, you are doing the opposite by frightening her.”
As the necessary medical tests continued, the assistant doctors said the unborn child had moved towards the upper part of the abdomen and would have to be delivered through an operation.
The couple still did not give up hope. They contacted the doctor who had treated them throughout the pregnancy and discussed the matter, but that brought no solution. Finally, at around 10:30pm, the woman gave birth through an operation.
From the beginning, the doctor had said he would make every possible effort for a normal delivery. The couple’s experience was different.
Their experience is one part of the overall picture of childbirth among women in the country. Every day, many women like her have to give birth through operations.
The caesarean rate in the country was 19.1% in 2012-13. In 2019, it increased to 36%. In 2025, it reached 51.8%.
The rate varies according to urban and rural areas and economic status. It is 56% in urban areas and 50% in rural areas. Among women from the wealthiest families, 68% give birth through caesarean sections. The rate is 57% in the fourth wealthiest group, 52% in the middle group and 34% among the poorest families.
According to the WHO, caesarean sections should not be performed without medical necessity. Although caesarean rates are increasing worldwide, this has not increased health benefits; rather, the risks for mothers and children have increased. The organisation says a caesarean rate of 10% to 15% at the population level is the most appropriate.
Dr Kishwar Sultana, professor of the Department of Gynaecology and Obstetrics at Holy Family Red Crescent Medical College and Hospital, told Dhaka Tribune there are multiple reasons behind the increase.
First, she said, it needs to be examined whether the rate is increasing more in the private or public sector. Some private-sector hospitals are still not being brought fully under monitoring, and some centres are operated for commercial purposes. However, this cannot be said about all institutions. In some cases, there may be a lack of proper supervision.
Another reason is that mothers who previously had a caesarean section also have to undergo caesarean sections for subsequent childbirths. Some mothers also think that they will have two children, so there is no need to go through the pain of normal delivery. This is called maternal choice.
Pointing out that some matters on the doctors’ side also need to be considered, she said the safety of mother and child is important to doctors. There is no guarantee that both will be fine simply because a normal delivery takes place, and the lengthy process of normal delivery also needs to be considered. Even then, doctors try for normal delivery, but many times patients’ families do not want to accept this. Whenever any problem occurs, the blame is placed on the doctor. No doctor wants anything bad to happen to their patient. However, there is no scope to deny that medical negligence has occurred in some cases, but it is also not right to hold all doctors responsible.
She said repeat caesarean sections are also a major reason. If a mother has a caesarean section once, a caesarean is also performed for her subsequent childbirth. Even for the delivery of a third or fourth child, a caesarean has to be performed. If someone has had two caesarean sections before and is pregnant again, it is assumed that she will have to undergo a caesarean for the third time as well. This is how the number is increasing.
Professor Sultana said that if a woman comes to a doctor and wants a normal delivery, it is her right. If everything is fine during pregnancy, she is advised accordingly, and they wait until the scheduled date. If labour pains do not begin even after that, it is possible to wait and observe for another two to four days, or even up to seven days, while the baby’s heartbeat is monitored.
However, caution is needed from the beginning in some pregnancies. If the mother’s blood pressure rises significantly, the condition of the unborn child deteriorates, the baby’s heartbeat becomes abnormal or the baby passes stool inside the womb, delivery has to be performed on an emergency basis. If the mother starts bleeding, quick measures also need to be taken. caesarean sections have to be performed in these cases. Hospitals with maternity services generally have arrangements for emergency caesarean sections 24 hours a day.
Professor Farhana Dewan, former president of the Obstetrical and Gynaecological Society of Bangladesh (OGSB), also told Dhaka Tribune that doctors try for normal delivery. It is not that caesarean sections are performed intentionally, she said, and many times patients also want them. However, there are many reasons why caesarean deliveries are more common than normal deliveries.
She said caesarean sections are sometimes necessary for medical reasons, for example if there has been a previous caesarean section, if the baby’s position is not correct, if the amniotic fluid decreases, if the baby’s movements decrease or if the mother has a tumour in her uterus. In such cases, a caesarean is performed through prior planning, which is called an elective caesarean. Even after labour pains begin, an emergency caesarean may be necessary for various reasons. These are the indications for caesarean sections, or medical reasons. If everything is normal, doctors try for normal delivery.
Decisions are sometimes taken considering the safety of the baby as well, she said. Doctors become concerned if the baby cannot be monitored properly or if there is a risk that the baby’s condition may deteriorate. Sometimes, if a caesarean is performed late, the baby may develop breathing difficulties, and there may even be a risk of death.
In an ideal situation, Professor Dewan said, every hospital should have a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), making it possible to provide medical support to newborns when necessary. However, the number of NICU facilities in the country is inadequate compared to the number of deliveries. Many people are unable to receive this service because they do not have the financial means, and beds are often unavailable in government hospitals as well.
In some risky situations, she said, the decision to perform a caesarean is made through prior planning. In other cases, an emergency caesarean has to be performed. For example, if a patient starts bleeding, it is an immediate emergency. Such caesarean sections cannot be performed just anywhere; they have to be performed at a multidisciplinary centre where the necessary facilities and various specialist doctors are available.
Another issue being seen more frequently is maternal request, meaning the mother herself wants a caesarean section. She directly says she will not be able to tolerate the pain of normal delivery and therefore wants a caesarean. This is not seen only in Bangladesh; it is also observed in different countries around the world.
Professor Dewan said mothers are kept under observation throughout pregnancy to determine whether they are prepared for normal delivery. Through regular check-ups, as the scheduled delivery date approaches, it is examined whether the mother has diabetes, high blood pressure or any other physical problem and whether the baby’s position is correct. If everything is fine, normal delivery can be attempted. However, if the mother’s age is very high or she has any other physical problem, additional caution needs to be taken when making the decision.
Professor Dewan said that even if the first child is born through a caesarean section, the second can be delivered through normal delivery. It is necessary, however, to know why the first child was not delivered through normal delivery and why a caesarean had to be performed. Doctors ask every patient about this. If there were reasons such as prolonged labour pains or the cervix not opening even after the scheduled date had passed, normal delivery can be attempted for the second child.
If the mother’s pelvis, or the passage through which the baby is born, is small, there is no possibility of normal delivery. Along with hearing the patient’s previous history, doctors try to understand why a caesarean was performed the first time by examining previous medical documents. If there is a recurring reason that will require a caesarean for subsequent childbirth as well, then it has to be performed. But if a caesarean had to be performed for a temporary reason, such as the baby’s heartbeat decreasing, the water breaking or the umbilical cord coming out first, normal delivery can be attempted for the second child.
At a workshop organised by the Bangladesh Midwifery Society (BMS) on July 6, Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain emphasised the importance of reducing the trend of unnecessary caesarean operations. He said delivery rooms must be established compulsorily at all private clinics and hospitals by July 11, otherwise the licences of the concerned institutions would be cancelled.
The minister said the trend had increased at an alarming rate. At present, he said, a section of people in the country has become excessively profit-oriented, with their main goal being to earn money rather than the welfare of people or the interests of the country. This has also had a negative impact on the healthcare sector.
He said that at one time, most children in the country were born through normal delivery, and there was a long tradition of safe childbirth in rural areas with the assistance of experienced traditional birth attendants. Although healthcare has improved now, the trend of unnecessary caesarean sections for commercial purposes has increased.
Initially, after regular medical examinations, in many cases broker networks and some medical centres frighten family members by warning them of various complications. They create fears such as, “If an operation is not performed, the mother or the child will not survive”, and force families to make the decision to undergo a caesarean section. Naturally, families fall into this trap because they do not want to take risks with the lives of the mother and child.
The minister also alleged that some private clinics and broker networks were encouraging pregnant women to undergo caesarean sections by frightening and intimidating them. He said the government would take strict measures to protect the nation from this situation. At the same time, 100,000 new personnel would be recruited in the health sector, of whom 80,000 would be women, most of them midwifery workers.
Overall, medical necessity, maternal choice, repeat caesarean sections, commercial tendencies among hospitals and limitations in healthcare facilities have emerged as factors behind the increase in the caesarean rate. According to experts, decisions must be made by considering the circumstances of each pregnancy. Creating opportunities for normal delivery by avoiding caesarean sections without medical necessity, and ensuring accountability among hospitals in this regard, are now major challenges.

item.title: Wahid-Uz-Zaman appointed new BTRC chairman
item.description:
Major General (retd) Md Wahid-Uz-Zaman has been appointed chairman of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) for one year on a contractual basis, replacing Major General Md Emdad Ul Bari.
The remaining tenure of Emdad Ul Bari's contractual appointment as BTRC chairman has been cancelled.
The Ministry of Public Administration issued two separate notifications in this regard on Sunday.
According to the notification on the new appointment, Wahid-Uz-Zaman has been appointed under Section 49 of the Government Service Act, 2018, subject to the suspension of his post-retirement leave and related benefits and relinquishment of any other professional or business engagement, as well as employment with any government, semi-government or private institution or organization.
He has been appointed on a contractual basis as commissioner (management and administration) of the BTRC and posted as its chairman for one year from the date of his joining.
Other terms and conditions of the appointment will be determined through a contract, the notification said.

item.title: BB to lift tenure limits on expatriate bonds to boost reserves
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has taken initiatives to collect foreign currency through Non-Resident Convertible (NRC) accounts and relax investment limits and tenure restrictions on three types of bonds introduced for expatriates to boost foreign exchange reserves.
At the same time, the central bank aims to set targets to reduce banks' corporate lending and increase loans in the retail and small and medium enterprise (SME) industries.
There is a plan to bring corporate loans down to 45 percent starting next year.
Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman disclosed these plans Saturday at the "5th Bangladesh Economic Summit-2026," organized by Bonik Barta at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in the capital.
The governor said that NRC accounts have already been launched, and the accounts are being promoted internationally with the assistance of the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
Through similar accounts, India raised $32 billion and Pakistan raised $13 billion within four to five months. Bangladesh also wants to collect foreign currency in this manner.
However, the central bank is also cautious to ensure that repayments under the NRC scheme over the next three to four years do not put major pressure on the reserves.
Noting that the tenure of the three types of bonds currently available to expatriates is capped at a maximum of 15 years, the governor said an initiative has been taken to lift this limit and make the tenure open-ended.
He mentioned that there is currently an investment equivalent to around $604 million to $606 million in these bonds. If the restrictions can be relaxed, more foreign currency will flow into the country, increasing reserves.
Meanwhile, the governor stated that 70% to 80% of private banks' loans are going to the corporate sector.
He said commercial bank licenses were not granted solely for corporate lending, and loan disbursement targets for this sector may be fixed for next year.
He urged bankers to disburse at least 20% of their loans to retail customers and 35% to the SME sector, while bringing the share of corporate loans down to 45%.
The governor added that arrangements must be made for large industrial enterprises to raise their necessary financing from the capital market. This will create purchasing power and demand in the economy and also make it easier for large industrial enterprises to survive.

item.title: Govt cuts import duties on dates, oranges and apples ahead of Ramadan
item.description:
The government on Sunday said import duties on imported dates, oranges, and apples would be reduced temporarily, coinciding with the holy month of Ramadan.
According to an official statement, the cabinet, in its 27th meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in the chair, decided to reduce duty on imported dates to 5% from 25%, while the rate would remain in effect until March 10, 2027.
It said the import tax on oranges (malta) under HS Code 08051010 and apples under HS Code 08081010 was set at 61%, down from the existing 121.78%, while the makeshift arrangement would remain effective from January 24 to February 23.
The statement said the cabinet gave in-principle and final approval to a revenue board (NBR) proposal to revert from the quarterly setup introduced in the 2026-27 budget, asking standard businesses to submit VAT returns within 15 days of the end of each monthly tax period.
The revised provision is expected to be incorporated in the proposed “Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty (Amendment) Act, 2026” amending an October 2026 ordinance introducing quarterly VAT filing with monthly submissions.
It recalled that the budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year had relaxed the requirement of submitting VAT returns every month, allowing submission within 15 days of the end of every three months in line with the ordinance.
The statement said the change created obstacles for revenue collection at the field level, making it necessary to amend Section 64 of the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012.
The amendment is expected to be approved at the current parliament session, subject to Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division vetting.
